1.why: The rule of law means everyone is regulated by law — individuals and governments alike. No person and no official is above the law.
1.tip: Rule of law cuts both ways: the state is bound by it too.

2.why: Magna Carta, signed in England in 1215, is the origin of Canada's tradition of ordered liberty — the Great Charter of Freedoms.
2.tip: Magna Carta, 1215 — about 800 years of ordered liberty.

3.why: Canadian law draws on English common law, the French Civil Code as used in Quebec, and Acts passed by Parliament. American federal law has no force in Canada.
3.tip: Three sources, all Canadian or British — nothing from the south.

5.why: The opening words of the Charter point to both Canada's religious traditions and the dignity and worth of the human person, alongside the rule of law.
5.tip: The preamble carries both ideas, so "both" is the safe read.

6.why: The tradition dates to Magna Carta in 1215, which is why the study guide describes it as roughly 800 years old.
6.tip: Same fact as Magna Carta, stated as a length of time.

7.why: Habeas corpus — the right to challenge unlawful detention — comes to Canada from English common law.

8.why: In the Oath of Citizenship you swear allegiance to the Sovereign — the King or Queen — not to a politician or an office-holder.
8.tip: Allegiance is to the Crown; the Prime Minister is never the answer.

9.why: Applicants aged 18 to 54 must show adequate knowledge of English or French and take the knowledge test.

10.why: The Governor General represents the Sovereign at the federal level; Lieutenant Governors do so in the provinces.
10.tip: Federal: Governor General. Provincial: Lieutenant Governor.

11.why: The 1982 amendment entrenched the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms in the Constitution.

12.why: Multiculturalism is recognised in the Constitution as a fundamental characteristic of Canada, to be respected and celebrated.
12.tip: It is protected nationally, not limited to one province.
